title: Hindley-Milner
description: Hindley-Milner infers the most general type of every expression with zero annotations: the identity function gets forall a. a -> a. Algorithm W walks the AST generating type variables and unifying them — when it sees f(x) it unifies f's type with (typeof x -> fresh var). The result is principal types: any valid typing is an instance of the inferred one. It is why ML and Haskell feel typed without writing types.
mechanism: Generate fresh type variables per subexpression; emit equality constraints from language constructs; solve by unification (union-find with occurs check); generalize free variables at let-bindings.
algo: Algorithm W is near-linear in practice (DEXPTIME pathological worst case). Unification is almost O(n alpha(n)).
demo:
# Hindley-Milner idea: generate type variables, unify constraints.
# identity: fn x -> x   gives   forall a. a -> a
class TVar:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
    def __repr__(self):
        return 't%d' % self.n

counter = [0]
def fresh():
    counter[0] += 1
    return TVar(counter[0])

# fn x -> x : arg type t1, result type t1  =>  t1 -> t1
arg = fresh()
print('fn x -> x  :  %s -> %s' % (arg, arg))
# fn f -> fn x -> f x : f : t2->t3, x : t2  =>  (t2->t3) -> t2 -> t3
f_t, x_t, r_t = fresh(), fresh(), fresh()
print('fn f -> fn x -> f x  :  (%s->%s) -> %s -> %s  (unified from constraints)' % (x_t, r_t, x_t, r_t))

title: Unification
description: Unification solves type equations: given t1 = List[t2] and t1 = List[int], it concludes t2 = int. The algorithm uses union-find over type terms — bind a variable to a term, follow bindings on lookup — with the occurs check rejecting infinite types (t = List[t] fails). Every inference engine, from Prolog to TypeScript, has a unifier at its core.
mechanism: Represent types as terms; union-find with path compression; unify(t1, t2): if same var, ok; if var, bind (after occurs check); if constructors, unify pairwise. Bindings accumulate into the substitution.
algo: Almost O(n alpha(n)) with union-find. Occurs check is the soundness guard against infinite types.

title: Constraint-based inference
description: Modern inference separates generation from solving: walk the AST emitting subtyping constraints (t1 <: t2), then solve the constraint set. This split lets one solver serve many language features — overloads, generics, variance — as different constraint kinds. TypeScript and Flow work this way; the solver is where the interesting errors (and the interesting bugs) live.
mechanism: Generate constraints per construct (call: arg <: param; return: declared vs inferred). Solve by propagation: upper/lower bounds per variable, iterate to fixpoint. Report the conflicting constraints on failure — that is the error message.
algo: Fixpoint iteration, O(constraints) typical. Error quality depends on tracking constraint provenance.

title: Type narrowing
description: Narrowing refines a variable's type from control flow: after 'if isinstance(x, str)', x is str inside the branch. Checkers track these facts per program point, joining them at merges (x is str|int after the if). It makes dynamic-language type checking feel smart — the checker follows the same reasoning a reader does. Discriminated unions and truthiness checks are the common patterns.
mechanism: Flow analysis: each statement transforms the type environment; isinstance/None checks add facts; joins take unions; assignments overwrite. Facts expire at function boundaries (conservative).
algo: O(program points * vars) flow analysis. Join is union; precision from path-sensitivity (bounded).
demo:
# narrowing: the checker's knowledge of x evolves through control flow
def describe(env, point):
    print('%-28s x: %s' % (point, env))

env = 'str | int'
describe(env, 'entry')
describe('str', 'after isinstance(x, str) == True')
describe('int', 'else branch')
describe('str | int', 'after merge (join = union)')
# None checks, the most common narrowing in practice:
print('if x is not None:  x: str   (was str | None)')
print('checkers track these facts per program point, like a careful reader')

title: Generics inference
description: Generics let one function serve many types: identity<T>(x: T): T. Inference fills in T from the arguments — no explicit type arguments needed at the call site. The engine collects constraints from each argument (T = typeof arg) and unifies them; conflicts ('expected T, got string vs int') become errors. Variance (covariant/contravariant) governs how generic types relate.
mechanism: Fresh inference variables per type parameter; constraints from arguments and return context; solve by unification; check bounds. Explicit arguments override inference.
algo: O(args) constraint collection + unification. Higher-rank types need annotations (undecidable in general).

title: Gradual typing
description: Gradual typing mixes typed and untyped code: annotated functions are checked statically, unannotated ones are dynamic (Any). The boundary is guarded — values crossing from dynamic to typed code are checked at runtime (or trusted, in the 'erasure' dialects). It lets codebases adopt types file by file, which is how Python and JS actually got typed in practice.
mechanism: Any is both top and bottom (compatible both ways, unsoundly). Static checking where annotations exist; runtime casts or trust at boundaries. Strictness flags ratchet the boundary tighter over time.
algo: Checking cost only for annotated code; unannotated is O(1) skip. Soundness is opt-in per dialect.
demo:
# gradual: checked where annotated, dynamic where not
def checked_add(a: int, b: int) -> int:  # statically checked
    return a + b

def dynamic_add(a, b):  # Any: unchecked
    return a + b

print('checked:', checked_add(1, 2))
print('dynamic:', dynamic_add('x', 'y'), '(Any flows anywhere: convenient, unsound)')
print('mypy --strict ratchets the boundary: fewer Anys, more checking')
print('migration path: annotate hot paths first, expand over time')

title: Flow-sensitive analysis
description: Flow-sensitive analysis tracks how types change statement by statement, unlike flow-insensitive analysis which merges everything. It knows x is int on line 5 and str on line 10 after reassignment. The cost is analyzing each program point; the payoff is precision that matches how developers actually read code. All production checkers for dynamic languages are flow-sensitive.
mechanism: Dataflow over the CFG: type environment in/out per statement; transfer functions per statement kind; join at merges. Reassignment updates the environment; the old type is forgotten (correctly).
algo: O(statements * vars); joins are unions. Loops need fixpoint iteration (usually 2-3 passes).
demo:
import ast

src = 'x = 1\nx = "hi"\ny = x\n'
env = {}
for node in ast.parse(src).body:
    if isinstance(node, ast.Assign):
        target = node.targets[0].id
        val = node.value
        t = 'int' if isinstance(val, ast.Constant) and isinstance(val.value, int) else \
            'str' if isinstance(val, ast.Constant) else env.get(val.id, '?')
        env[target] = t
        print('line %d: x is now %s (flow-sensitive: statement-by-statement)' % (node.lineno, t))
print('final env:', env, '(flow-insensitive would say x: int|str everywhere)')

title: Occurs check and infinite types
description: The occurs check is unification's safety valve: it rejects t = List[t], which would be an infinite type. Without it, the unifier loops forever or builds a cyclic structure that crashes later passes. Most production unifiers implement it — the cost is a traversal per binding, negligible against the bugs it prevents. It is the difference between 'type error' and 'compiler hang'.
mechanism: Before binding variable v to term t, check v does not occur in t (recursive scan). If it does, fail with a proper type error instead of looping.
algo: O(term size) per binding. Prolog famously skips it for speed — and gets infinite terms.
demo:
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(100)

# what happens WITHOUT the occurs check: infinite structure
class T:
    pass

t = T()
try:
    t.inner = ('List', t)  # t = List[t]: cyclic!
    def depth(x, seen=0):
        return depth(x[1], seen + 1) if isinstance(x, tuple) else seen
    print('depth:', depth(t.inner))
except RecursionError:
    print('RecursionError: printing the infinite type blows the stack')
print('the occurs check turns this into a clean type error instead')

title: Polymorphic let-bindings
description: Let-polymorphism is what makes 'let id = fn x -> x in (id 1, id "s")' typecheck: the bound variable gets a type scheme (forall a. a -> a), and each use instantiates fresh variables. Without generalization, id would be monomorphic and the second use would fail. The value restriction (only syntactic values generalize) keeps this sound in the presence of mutation.
mechanism: At let x = e: infer e's type, generalize free variables into a scheme. At each use of x: instantiate the scheme with fresh variables. Value restriction: generalize only values, not arbitrary expressions.
algo: Generalization O(free vars); instantiation O(scheme size) per use.
demo:
# let-polymorphism: one definition, used at two types
# let id = fn x -> x   :   forall a. a -> a
# use 1: id 1      instantiates a := int
# use 2: id 's'    instantiates a := str  (fresh variables each use!)

def identity(x):
    return x

print(identity(1), identity('s'))  # same function, two types: no annotations needed
print('each use instantiates the scheme with FRESH variables')
print('value restriction: only syntactic values generalize (mutation stays sound)')

title: Inference in IDEs
description: IDEs run inference continuously and incrementally: hover shows the inferred type, completions filter by it, and red squiggles appear as you type. The engine must be fast (keystroke latency), incremental (re-infer only the edited region's dependents), and resilient (partial results for broken code). Pyright and rust-analyzer proved it scales to million-line codebases in an editor.
mechanism: Incremental inference with dependency tracking: edit -> find affected definitions -> re-infer in topological order -> publish diagnostics. Query APIs (hover, completion) read the latest results without blocking.
algo: O(affected) re-inference per edit; queries O(1) over cached results.
demo:
# IDE view: inferred types available for hover/completion without annotations
import ast

src = 'def total(xs):\n    return sum(xs)\n\nresult = total([1, 2])\n'
tree = ast.parse(src)

# crude inference: return type from the returned expression
for node in ast.walk(tree):
    if isinstance(node, ast.FunctionDef):
        ret = [n for n in ast.walk(node) if isinstance(n, ast.Return)]
        print('hover total -> inferred: def total(xs: ?) -> int  (from `return sum(xs)`)')
print('hover result -> int (from the call)')
print('IDEs do this incrementally, per keystroke, for the whole codebase')

title: Good type error messages
description: Inference is only as good as its errors: 'expected int, got str at argument 2 of total (called from main line 42)' beats 'unification failed'. Good messages track constraint provenance (which expression created each constraint), blame the right location (the argument, not the function), and suggest fixes. Error quality is the top predictor of whether developers adopt a type system.
mechanism: Tag each constraint with its source span; on conflict, walk back to the blamed spans; render expected-vs-actual with the relevant code snippets. Elm's compiler is the gold standard for message design.
algo: Provenance tracking is O(constraints) memory; message rendering is O(blamed spans).
demo:
# constraint provenance -> blamed location in the message
constraints = [
    {'eq': ('t_arg', 'int'), 'src': 'main.py:42 (argument 2)'},
    {'eq': ('t_arg', 'str'), 'src': 'main.py:42 (argument 2 value "x")'},
    {'eq': ('t_param', 'int'), 'src': 'lib.py:7 (parameter of total)'},
]
print('error: argument 2 of total() has incompatible type')
print('  expected: int   (lib.py:7: parameter of total)')
print('  got     : str   (main.py:42: argument 2 value "x")')
print('blame the argument, show both sides, cite both locations')

title: Soundness vs completeness
description: Soundness means 'no false negatives' (every reported program is truly wrong); completeness means 'no false positives' (every wrong program is reported). Real checkers choose: sound but incomplete (rejects some valid programs — Haskell), or complete-ish but unsound (accepts some wrong ones — TypeScript, mypy with Any). The choice shapes the ecosystem: soundness for compilers, pragmatism for gradual adoption.
mechanism: Sound: conservative rules (no Any escape hatches). Pragmatic: Any/dynamic as the pressure valve, strictness flags to tighten. Document which the checker promises — users build workflows on it.
algo: A design decision with engineering consequences, not a runtime algorithm.
demo:
# unsoundness via Any: the checker trusts you, the runtime disagrees
def get_name(user: dict) -> str:
    return user['name']

user: dict = {'name': 'Ada'}          # typed: fine
mystery = {}                          # Any: unchecked
mystery['name'] = 42                  # no error: Any flows anywhere
print('typed path:', get_name(user))
try:
    print('any path  :', get_name(mystery).upper())
except AttributeError as e:
    print('runtime error the checker missed:', e)
print('soundness = no missed errors; completeness = no false alarms; pick per project')

title: Higher-ranked types
description: Rank-1 polymorphism (forall at the top level) covers most code, but some patterns need forall inside: a function taking a polymorphic function as an argument. Higher-rank types require annotations — inference is undecidable in general — but they express things rank-1 cannot, like ST-monad encapsulation. Most developers never write them; library authors occasionally must.
mechanism: Annotation-guided: the declared higher-rank type drives checking (bidirectional inference); unannotated code stays rank-1. GHC's RankNTypes is the canonical implementation.
algo: Decidable with annotations (bidirectional); undecidable without. Rare in application code.
demo:
# rank-2: takes a POLYMORPHIC function (works at every type), not a monomorphic one
# apply_poly :: (forall a. a -> a) -> (Int, String)
# apply_poly f = (f 1, f 'x')
# rank-1 cannot express this: f would be fixed to one type

def apply_poly(f):
    return (f(1), f('x'))  # f used at Int AND String: must be polymorphic

print(apply_poly(lambda x: x))
print('needs an annotation in Haskell (RankNTypes); inference alone is undecidable here')

title: Effect systems
description: Effect systems track what code does, not just what it returns: which functions do I/O, throw, or mutate. They generalize checked exceptions into a compositional algebra — the type of 'reads a file' differs from 'pure computation'. Koka, Effekt, and OCaml 5's handlers make effects explicit; the payoff is reasoning ('this refactor cannot break I/O behavior') and optimization (pure code reorders freely).
mechanism: Effect rows/variables like type variables; unification over effects; handlers interpret effects (like catch for exceptions, generalized). Inference extends HM with effect constraints.
algo: Effect inference parallels type inference; handlers add interpretation cost at runtime.
demo:
# effects as values: track what code DOES in the type
# pure   : Int -> Int
# throws : Int -> Int throws IO
# Python sketch: annotate effects, check composition
EFFECTS = {'read_file': {'io'}, 'parse': set(), 'save': {'io', 'throws'}}

def effect_of(calls):
    eff = set()
    for c in calls:
        eff |= EFFECTS[c]
    return eff

print('parse:', effect_of(['parse']), '(pure: reorders freely, caches safely)')
print('pipeline:', effect_of(['read_file', 'parse', 'save']))
print('the type tells you what it does, not just what it returns')

title: Inference performance
description: Inference must be fast enough to run on every keystroke: budgets are ~100ms for the edited file's closure. The techniques are incremental re-inference, lazy constraint solving (solve only what hover/completion asks about), and caching solved constraints per definition. Pathological cases (deeply nested generics, huge tuple types) get recursion limits and 'type too complex' bailouts instead of hangs.
mechanism: Dependency-ordered re-inference; demand-driven solving; memoize per-definition results keyed by content hash; fuel limits on expansion (e.g., 100k steps) with graceful degradation.
algo: O(affected) incremental; fuel-bounded worst case. Profiling flags find the slow definitions.
demo:
import time

# demand-driven: solve only what the query asks about
solved = {}

def infer(name, depth=0):
    if name in solved:
        return solved[name]  # memoized
    time.sleep(0.001 * (depth + 1))  # fake work
    solved[name] = 'type-of-' + name
    return solved[name]

t = time.perf_counter()
infer('hover_target')  # user hovers ONE symbol: solve one, not the file
print('hover answered in %.1fms (demand-driven, memoized)' % ((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000))
print('fuel limits + bailouts keep pathological generics from hanging the IDE')
